title: The wide permitted
hookLine: most of life is simply permitted

lines: LEAVE ME AS I LEAVE YOU.
cards: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells the people that Allah has made the pilgrimage a duty for them. A man calls out: every year, Messenger of Allah? The Prophet stays silent.

The man asks again, and again. Finally the answer comes, in Sahih Muslim: if I said yes, it would become a duty every year, and you would not be able to do it. Then a request: leave me as I leave you.
Don't go hunting for burdens nobody placed on you. Today's word is the space that request protects.

teach.b: The word is mubah, permitted, the middle of yesterday's dial. No reward for doing it, no blame for leaving it.

Jurists have a principle about it that changes how the whole law feels: in things and in dealings, the starting point is permission. Something is permitted unless a text forbids it, not the other way round.
The Qur'an says, in Surah al-Baqarah: "He it is Who created for you all that is in the earth." For you. The food, the trade, the clothes, the games, the jokes, the long walk at dusk.
Jurists start from yes, and ask for evidence before they say no. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari puts the warning sharply.
The Prophet says the Muslim with the greatest guilt is the one who asks about something that wasn't forbidden, and it becomes forbidden because of his asking. Asking isn't the problem in that report.
Inventing burdens is. Now one turn, so this isn't misread. The starting point flips for worship.

teach.h: WORSHIP STARTS FROM WHAT WAS TAUGHT.
teach.b: Jurists say a new act of worship needs a text behind it, because worship is offered the way it was taught. In prayer, start from what was taught. In the market, the kitchen and the park, start from permitted.

Put those together and the forbidden becomes a list, and the permitted a wide field. A person can spend most of a day in the field, eating, working, laughing, resting, and none of it is outside the law.
Some of it can even become worship, jurists add, when it's done with a good intention.

how: Muslim jurists generally start from permission in food, trade and everyday life, asking for evidence before calling something forbidden, while acts of worship follow what was taught.

o: recommended: rewarded if done, but no blame if left undone
allowed only after a scholar gives a written ruling
simply permitted: no reward for doing it, no blame for leaving it

games.q: the wide permitted — tap the pairs.
p: leave me as I leave you

s: in Islamic law, things are forbidden until a text allows them
in things and dealings, the starting point is permission; a text is needed to forbid.
the Prophet warned about asking until something permitted became forbidden
a report in Sahih al-Bukhari says so.
the starting point of permission applies to new acts of worship too
jurists say worship follows what was taught.

games.q: the Prophet says pilgrimage is a duty. a man keeps asking: every year? what does the Prophet say?
o: yes, every year, for everyone able.
if I said yes, it would become a duty, and you couldn't do it.
games.why: he stayed silent, then said a yes would have made it a duty every year. leave me as I leave you.

practice: Choose something small that's simply allowed, a cup of tea, bread still warm, the sound outside your window, a stretch, and do it now, or hold it in your mind. Don't turn it into a task; let it be a good thing in the wide field.
If you pray, you can thank Allah for it.

wordCard.voice: Mubah. Permitted: no reward for doing it, no blame for leaving it, and in things and dealings, the starting point. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: permitted, allowed; the middle of the five rulings.

carryVoice: Your line: most is permitted. A good thing, in the wide field, with no permission slip needed. Go gently.
